title: Adaptive Information Mining: Approaching the Quantum Limit of Super-Resolution Imaging
authors: Seungman Choi, Peter Menart, Andrew Schramka, Zubin Jacob
abstract: The "Rayleigh limit" is not an intrinsic property of light, but a consequence of sub-optimal measurement of collected photons by the imaging instrument. To overcome this limitation, we present Adaptive Information Mining, a framework that achieves super-resolution by using sequentially refined measurements for incoming photons. Our approach employs a reconfigurable imaging system that dynamically reshapes the instrument measurement responses to maximize the Fisher information and guide scene estimation toward the fundamental quantum limit, even in deep sub-Rayleigh regimes. We demonstrate that this approach achieves an estimation error 2-5 times closer to the fundamental quantum limit than traditional direct imaging when imaging point sources, without requiring any prior knowledge of their positions and brightnesses. Importantly, we demonstrate that AIM can be extended to fully blind multi-parameter estimation in scenarios involving an unknown number of sources or turbulence-induced wavefront distortions. Our approach addresses the limitations of conventional fixed imaging, offering a practical path toward quantum-limited super-resolution imaging.
summary: This paper introduces Adaptive Information Mining (AIM), a novel framework for achieving super-resolution imaging by treating measurement design as an active optimization problem. By iteratively designing measurement patterns to maximize Fisher information, AIM overcomes the limitations of passive imaging, pushing estimation precision toward the fundamental quantum limit. This has practical implications for high-precision scientific instrumentation like astronomy.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental limitation of super-resolution imaging imposed by the Rayleigh limit, arguing it stems from sub-optimal measurement rather than intrinsic physics.
main_result: The proposed Adaptive Information Mining (AIM) framework achieves super-resolution by actively designing sequential measurements to drive estimation error significantly closer to the fundamental quantum limit than traditional direct imaging.
method: AIM employs a closed-loop, information-driven cycle where the next measurement pattern is optimized to maximize the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), thereby minimizing the uncertainty ellipsoid volume.
model_or_system: The system involves reconfigurable imaging hardware, specifically using Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) to dynamically shape the measurement response for incoming photons from point sources.
key_observables: Estimation error (RMSE), Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), Quantum Cramer-Rao Lower Bound (QCRLB), and the ability to estimate unknown source numbers or wavefront distortions.
important_parameters: Super-resolution regime, deep sub-Rayleigh separation, photon count, and detector read noise levels.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is the ability to adaptively control the measurement system using reconfigurable interfaces (SLMs) based on current estimates.
figures_summary: Figures compare AIM vs. Direct Imaging (DI) performance across varying source separations and photon counts, demonstrating AIM's superior convergence toward the quantum limit. Other figures illustrate the iterative process and turbulence compensation.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the AIM framework (iterative optimization using FIM maximization), presents results comparing AIM to DI under various noise and source conditions, and discusses extensions to turbulence and unknown source numbers.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, information-theoretic framework for active quantum measurement, which has parallels in quantum control and optimal state estimation in open quantum systems.

Fig. 2. Adaptive Information Mining (AIM) for sub-Rayleigh imaging. (A) AIM operating principle. The AIM module (𝚽𝑡) is adaptively modulated based on prior measurements to drive the subsequent measurement toward high-information states. (B) Temporally evolving AIM framework compared to conventional direct imaging (DI). Dual SLMs placed after the imaging lens enable adaptive, scene-dependent measurements for resolving sub-Rayleigh point sources.

Fig. 3. Iterative workflow and temporal evolution of AIM estimation. (A) Closed-loop AIM workflow. An initial measurement is followed by a three-step iterative cycle— source estimation, information-driven SLM design, and subsequent measurement— enabling sub-Rayleigh imaging. (B) Temporal evolution of AIM estimation. Optimized dual-SLM phase masks Γ(1) and Γ(2), and corresponding measurements adapt over time to capture high-information states, enabling progressive convergence of estimated source positions (blue crosses) toward the ground truth (white circles).

Fig. 4. Inter-source overlap suppression via AIM for a three point source scene with brightness ratios [1: 3: 6]. Columns 1-2: optimized SLM phase patterns after convergence for different separations. Columns 3-4: source-resolved responses under AIM and DI (color-coded). Columns 5: inter-source correlation matrices, where off- diagonal elements quantify inter-source correlation, highlighting the overlap reduction achieved by AIM.

Fig. 5. Super-resolution performance of AIM using five sequential measurements, with position and brightness RMSE plotted as a function of source separation. Errors are averaged across three sources from 50 Monte Carlo trials per condition (Red cross). Yellow and red curves represent the classical CRLB for DI and AIM, respectively, while the gray curves denote the fundamental quantum CRLB. All results correspond to brightness ratios [1: 5: 20] and a total photon budget of 14,000. The total photon budget is equally distributed across each AIM measurement.
